children: CEO George Kurtz is pushing back against calls to slow frontier AI development, arguing that the cybersecurity threat investors should worry about is not theoretical or years away. His warning sharpens CrowdStrike's investment thesis: increasingly capable AI could make cyberattacks cheaper, faster and accessible to far more attackers, potentially expanding long-term demand for the company's security platform.
The genie's out of the bottle, Kurtz said, pointing to advanced and open-weight models already available.
Pacing what comes next doesn't secure what's already here, he added in response to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has called for slowing development of advanced AI.
Kurtz said AI is giving every criminal and lone actor elite execution, potentially allowing less-skilled attackers to operate with capabilities previously limited to sophisticated cyber groups.

His proposed response centers on security rather than slowing innovation. Kurtz said AI agents should be treated as privileged identities, with tightly controlled permissions, short-lived credentials and a kill switch. Humans should remain involved in high-stakes decisions.
He also called for closer cooperation between cybersecurity companies and AI developers including Anthropic and OpenAI, offering CrowdStrike's threat intelligence to independent evaluation efforts.

For investors, that argument arrives while CrowdStrike's underlying business is accelerating. Fiscal second-quarter revenue rose 26% to $1.47 billion, while annual recurring revenue climbed 25% to $5.84 billion. Record net new ARR reached $333 million, up 51%, and free cash flow totaled $377 million. CrowdStrike also raised its fiscal-2027 net-new-ARR growth outlook.
What CrowdStrike investors should watch next
The key question is whether rising AI-related security concerns translate into measurable platform expansion rather than simply stronger cybersecurity rhetoric.

Investors should watch net new ARR, Falcon Flex adoption, customer spending on identity and AI security, and free cash flow. CrowdStrike already generates more than $2.29 billion of ARR from customers using Falcon Flex, giving it a large installed base to cross-sell additional protection.
If autonomous agents dramatically expand the number of identities and endpoints companies must secure, Kurtz's warning could also describe one of CrowdStrike's largest future growth opportunities.

title: CrowdStrike CEO Warns AI Cyber Threat Is Already Here
